memo_script:
Picture this.

You've just eaten. The plate is clean. The auntie who cooked is watching you from the corner of the room — she's pretending to arrange something on the counter, but she's watching.

In England, you say "that was delicious." Nice. Polite. Forgotten by morning.

In a Coimbatore kitchen, you say: ரொம்ப பிடிச்சிருக்கு.

ரொம்ப — so much, really, deeply. பிடிச்சிருக்கு — it has grabbed me. It has *caught* me and won't let go.

Not "I liked it." Not "it was good." The food reached across the plate and took hold of something in you. That's what you're telling her.

And here's the thing about Tamil aunties and food — cooking is not just cooking. It's years of learning her mother-in-law's hand, the exact ratio of chilli to coriander her family expects, the pride that goes into every pot. When you say ரொம்ப பிடிச்சிருக்கு, you're not reviewing a dish. You're telling her the years landed.

Your wife's family is going to put food in front of you approximately every forty-five minutes. This phrase is your single most powerful tool in that house.

ரொம்ப பிடிச்சிருக்கு. Romba pidichirukku.

Hold that. You'll know exactly when.

body: 🎙️ The Tamil word that says 'done and dusted' — ஆயிட்டேன். 90 sec, no homework.
memo_script:
So there's this little suffix that Tamil speakers stick onto almost everything — and once you hear it, you'll hear it everywhere.

It's -இட்டு. Or in fast speech, just -ட்டு. And it means the thing is *done*. Finished. Off you go.

வந்துட்டேன் — I've arrived, I'm here, done.
கழுவிட்டு வரேன் — let me wash up and I'll come, I'll be right there.
ஆயிட்டேன் — I'm ready, sorted, done.
விட்டுடு — just let it go, leave it, it's over.

Native speakers don't decide to add it. It just *falls out*. It's the sound of wrapping something up without making a big deal of it. Very Coimbatore — we don't linger on the transition, we just move.

The English cousin is 'I've gone and done it' — but we do it in one breath, not five words.

You already have seven deck items that live inside this pattern. Next time you see ட்டு at the end of something, you'll know exactly what it's doing.

No homework. Just let it sit.

body: 🎙️ One suffix does the work of in/at/on/over-the-phone — and you already said it at dinner.
memo_script:
You already used this one. At dinner, two weeks ago, you said 'Canada-la irukkom' — Canada-ல இருக்கோம். That ல at the end? That's the whole thing.

In Tamil, there's no separate word for 'in', 'at', or 'on'. You just stick ல onto the noun and you're done. வீட்ல — at home. போன்ல — on the phone. தமிழ்ல — in Tamil. கனடாவுல — in Canada. Same suffix, every time. The whole locative case, one sound.

Now here's the part I love. This suffix is so old, linguists trace it back over two thousand years — it shows up in Sangam poetry, same form, same job. The world changed, the word didn't. While English was still sorting out whether to say 'in' or 'at' or 'on' depending on context, Tamil had already decided: ல. Done.

And you'll hear it bent a little in Coimbatore. வீட்ல sometimes becomes வீட்லே — a tiny stretch, more feeling in it. Like you're really home. Same meaning, just warmer.

You're already saying it. You just didn't know what you were saying.

body: 🎙️ you asked about that -om ending — iruppom, pairom, saapiduvom. one suffix does the work of 'we've decided.' 90 seconds.
memo_script:
You asked about the ending on ஒரு மாசம் இருப்போம் — that last syllable, -om.

Tamil verbs carry the person right inside them. Not a separate word like 'we' stuck on front — the verb itself changes shape to say who's doing it. And -om is the shape it takes when it's *we, together, and it's settled*.

இருப்போம் — we'll be staying. Not 'maybe we'll stay.' Not 'we are staying.' *We'll be there* — committed, collective, done.

The same -om runs through everything:

சாப்பிடுவோம் — we'll eat.

போவோம் — let's go.

பாப்போம் — we'll see.

Listen for it at the table. When your maama says போவோம், he's not asking — he's announcing. The car is already started in his head.

So ஒரு மாசம் இருப்போம் — that's not 'we're planning to stay one month.' That's 'one month — we're there.' The -om is the full stop.

One suffix. Whole vibe.

body: 🎙️ the word that means 'it happened, move on' — ஆச்சு. one ending, a hundred situations. 60 sec.
memo_script:
ok so you know how in English you say 'it's done' or 'that happened' or 'time's up' — three different sentences for three different things?

Tamil does all of that with one ending: ஆச்சு.

யாரோ வந்தாங்க, சாப்பிட்டோம், போனோம் — and then: நேரம் ஆச்சு. time happened. it's time. we go.

Or the food's ready: சமைச்சாச்சு. the cooking became-done.

Or your maama is waving you off after the meal: ஆச்சு ஆச்சு — done done, enough, go sit.

The pattern: take any verb and push ச்சு onto the end. போ becomes போச்சு — it went, it's gone, that chapter closed. முடி becomes முடிஞ்சுச்சு — finished-happened.

The soul of it: ஆச்சு doesn't just report the past. it *closes* it. the thing landed. we move now.

And here's the one you'll hear most in that house: நேரம் ஆச்சு — time happened. said exactly the way your maama says 'alright then' and stands up from the chair. you'll know it the first second you hear it.

body: 🎙️ the word hiding inside 'I'm done' — வந்துட்டேன், ஆயிட்டேன், விட்டுடு — one suffix, every completion
memo_script:
ok da — you know that feeling when something's finished and you're already moving on? Tamil has one suffix that does exactly that.

It's -இட்டு. Or in fast speech, just -ட்டு. Stuck onto a verb, it means: done. already happened. move on.

வந்துட்டேன் — I came (and I'm here, it's done). கழுவிட்டு வரேன் — I'll wash up and come (wash: done, coming: next). ஆயிட்டேன் — I'm ready, I'm done, we're good.

The beautiful thing? It isn't just 'finished' like a past tense. It has attitude. It says: that chapter closed, this chapter opened. The completive already sitting inside seven items in your deck — pazhagippochu, vandhutten, ayitten — they all run on this same engine.

விட்டுடு — let it go, drop it, done with it. One word. Kongu Tamil runs on this suffix because the whole dialect has this energy: say it, do it, move on, don't fuss.

Next time you hear someone say வந்துட்டாங்க — they're here and it's settled, no drama. You already know what's powering it.
